title: Climate change impact assessment on water resources in the mountainous Karaj Dam Basin using an integrated weather generator-machine learning framework
abstract: This study assesses the impacts of climate change on water resources and droughts in the Karaj Dam basin, a key water source for Tehran, Iran. Sixteen climate projections from four GCMs under four SSPs were downscaled using the M-LARS-WG model. Monthly streamflow was simulated using the Random Forest (RF) model, with NSE of 0.96 (calibration) and 0.95 (validation). The models demonstrated strong performance in reproducing weather, streamflow, and drought characteristics, with droughts assessed by SPI, SPEI, and SDI indices. Under the median of future projections, annual streamflow and precipitation rise by ~ 4%, from 12.7 to 13.3 m3/s and 687 to 714 mm, while the probability of moderate or more intense droughts decreases by 3–4% (e.g., from 0.16 to 0.13 based on SPEI). Rising temperatures and increased snowmelt are expected to alter seasonal streamflow more than precipitation, leading to higher winter flows and lower spring flows. Based on the 12-month SDI, average drought duration and magnitude are projected to decrease from 23.4 months and 22.8 to 20.6 months and 20.2, respectively. These findings for the Karaj basin—due to differences in baseline climate conditions—contrast with projections for Tehran, alleviating concerns over severe future water shortages in the capital.
field: Climate change impacts on water resources
problem: Conventional weather generators underestimate inter-annual climate variability, a critical limitation for reliable drought studies, necessitating an integrated modeling framework to accurately assess climate change impacts on crucial water resources like the Karaj Dam basin.
method: This study proposes an integrated framework that couples a weather generator (M-LARS-WG) with a machine learning model (Random Forest) to simulate future streamflow and assess climate change impacts on water resources and hydrological droughts.
task: The task is to project climate change impacts on water resources and droughts in the Karaj Dam Basin, Iran, by integrating a weather generator to downscale climate scenarios with a machine learning model to simulate streamflow.
innovation: This study presents the first application of coupling the M-LARS-WG weather generator with a machine learning rainfall-runoff model to assess the impacts of climate change on hydrological droughts and water resources.

Moreover, Iran, located in a dryland region, has experienced severe water shortages and prolonged droughts, significantly affecting socioeconomic conditions, groundwater, and agricultural production 7. Over recent decades, most of the country's major basins have shown a persistent decline in runoff and water storage 2. About 25% of Tehran's water demand, with a population of around 10 million, is supplied by Karaj Dam 8, whose basin lies in a mountainous region. Therefore, assessing the impacts of climate change on the water resources of this basin using appropriate methods is of critical importance.

The M-LARS-WG model 23, a modified version of LARS-WG, is a daily WG whose structure has been modified to accurately reproduce inter-annual variability. These modifications have improved the model's ability to accurately reproduce key meteorological characteristics and to downscale GCM outputs 6,23,24. Despite the expected capability of this model for drought studies, it is being used for the first time in this study to assess the impacts of climate change on streamflow-related droughts. Its performance is compared with the LARS-WG model, which has been widely used in numerous studies to evaluate the impacts of climate change on drought 19-22.

To model the observed daily Tmax and Tmin series, the daily mean and standard deviation cycles of Tmax and Tmin are reduced separately for wet and dry days. A first-order multivariate autoregressive model (AR(1)) is then applied to the standardized residuals to capture the auto-correlation and cross-correlation between these variables. The daily AR(1) model is subsequently used to generate synthetic standardized Tmax and Tmin series, which are later de-standardized based on the mean and standard deviation cycles corresponding to rainfall occurrence. More information about the LARS-WG model can be found in Semenov and Stratonovitch (2010).

To correct for inter-annual variability in precipitation, the quantile perturbation method (QPM) is employed so that the generated monthly precipitation distribution aligns with the observed monthly precipitation

The correction of inter-annual variability in the Tmin and Tmax series is performed using a tri-variate AR(1) model, whose parameters are estimated by fitting to the observed monthly series. The monthly precipitation series is obtained by aggregating the daily precipitation series. Then, the monthly Tmin and Tmax series are generated using the monthly AR(1) model as dependent variables of the monthly precipitation series. Subsequently, the monthly means of Tmin and Tmax in the daily series are adjusted to match the corresponding values generated by the monthly model. This approach ensures that the statistical characteristics at the monthly timescale, derived from the outputs of the daily model, are consistent with those of the monthly model, thereby correcting inter-annual temperature variability. A detailed description of the M-LARS-WG model is provided in Khazaei et al. (2020) 23.

Random Forest (RF), introduced by Breiman (2001) 43, is a supervised machine learning algorithm and a powerful ensemble method for classification and regression. It constructs multiple decision trees using bootstrap resampling. The key advantage of ensemble learning is that combining multiple models improves accuracy compared to individual models 30. Each decision tree is built independently. At each node, the optimal split is selected from a randomly chosen subset of input variables rather than considering all features 44. This strategy reduces correlation among trees, enhancing predictive performance. The final prediction is obtained by majority voting in classification tasks or averaging in regression tasks 45.

For all AI-based models, hyperparameter tuning and optimization were performed using the 16-year training dataset. The RF model hyperparameters were tuned using Bayesian optimization in MATLAB. The final configuration consisted of 72 decision trees, with three predictors randomly selected at each node split. Model complexity was controlled through optimized constraints, including a minimum leaf size of 1 and a maximum of 116 splits per tree. For the ANN model, both structural and training hyperparameters were optimized using MATLAB's Bayesian optimization routine. A feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer was adopted, with an optimal architecture of five neurons in the hidden layer. Training was conducted for a maximum of 109 epochs with a learning rate of 0.0075, and early stopping was employed to prevent overfitting. For the SVM model, key hyperparameters were optimized using MATLAB's built-in optimization routine within a support vector regression (SVR) framework. A Gaussian (RBF) kernel was used, and the optimized parameters included a box constraint of 157.2, an epsilon-insensitive loss value of 0.1405, and a kernel scale of 194.0. Model training was performed using the sequential minimal optimization (SMO) algorithm. For the GLM, the selection of the distribution family and link function was guided by exploratory analysis of the training dataset, and the final configuration was chosen based on goodness- of-fit criteria and minimization of training error. Detailed results of the optimized GLM, including coefficients, standard errors, and statistical significance levels, are provided in Table S2 (Supporting Information). The independent 5-year dataset was reserved exclusively for final performance evaluation.

The calibration and validation results of the four rainfall-runoff models (RF, GLM, ANN, and SVM) are presented in Table 2. Among these, RF, SVM, and ANN demonstrated the best performance, with NSE and R² values exceeding 0.94 in both calibration and validation. Notably, RF achieved the highest performance during the calibration phase (NSE = 0.964, R2 = 0.965), whereas SVM outperformed all models in the validation phase (NSE = 0.970, R2 = 0.976). The ANN model also performed well, achieving NSE and R2 values of 0.948 during calibration and 0.950 and 0.959 during validation, respectively. In contrast, the GLM model showed only moderate accuracy in both calibration and validation (NSE ≈ 0.85).

To evaluate the performance of the models, the generated and observed monthly series were compared for each month using the t-test, F-test, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test. These tests assess differences in means, standard deviations, and probability distributions, respectively. Table 3 presents the number of rejected tests at the 5% significance level for each variable and model.
